results.content: In acceptance criteria and evidence of milestone completion sections number things in a corresponding way. It should describe a way by which it could be judged that output has been achieved, e.g. for a milestone relating to creation of video lectures, acceptance criteria might be to release 10 instructional videos per month. * Use the same number as used in the output section, so that it would be easy to understand that this acceptance criteria refers to this specific output. Evidence is linked to your output and acceptance criteria, e.g. output is video lectures, acceptance criteria is to release 10 instructional videos per month and evidence for it will be instructional videos posted on Youtube channel. * Make sure your evidence proves what you stated in outputs and acceptance criteria sections. * Use the same number for evidence of the specific output as you used in the outputs and acceptance criteria section, so that it would be easy to understand that all of them are connected.

results.content: Home Community Discussion Forums Most Active Software Boards LabVIEW Topic. # LabVIEW. * Float this Topic for Current User. ## FPGA : Multiply Adder IPCore latency. ## FPGA : Multiply Adder IPCore latency. ‎07-19-2016 07:55 AM - edited ‎07-19-2016 07:55 AM. If I set A to unsigned, the Latency is 4 and 3. I don't get this difference. I thought the DSPs were capable of handling 25x8 Multiplications and 48 bit adds in a single step. Why does switching between signed and unsigned for 25 bit lead to a difference in latency. If I set the bit width of A to 24, both signed and unsigned require 3 and 2 clock cycles to complete. ## Re: FPGA : Multiply Adder IPCore latency. ## Re: FPGA : Multiply Adder IPCore latency. So, if you get more, implementation is probably switched internally to multiple DSPs (page 6). Notice that all the DSP48  specifications say that they have two's complement multipliers - which are signed. Lets take Spartan-6 and DSP48A1 for example:  , page 6: "18-bit x 18-bit, two’s-complement multiplier". If you're using unsigned type, you're actually using one more bit which is normally sign bit (so single DPS is doing fine with 17-bit x17-bit unsigned inputs, or 18-bit signed x 17-bit unsigned). For comparison, DSP48E1 on Virtex-7 and Kintex-7 ( , page 9) and DSP48E on Virtex-5 ( ) have "25 × 18 two’s-complement multiplier". I assume you're using one of those, as your signed configuration have AB=3 and C=2, so - going back to the beggining of this post - you're fitting in one DSP slice. When you switch to unsigned, you're over the DSP multiplying capabilities. You can try to configure Multiplier and Adder Subtracter cores to see how many resources they use, and their sum should tell you about your Multiply Adder. ## Re: FPGA : Multiply Adder IPCore latency. ‎07-19-2016 04:42 PM. ## Re: FPGA : Multiply Adder IPCore latency. OK, so that means I'm using two cascaded DSPs for what I thought would only require a single DSP. Well that would explain it actually, the DSP treating the unsigned version as a 26-bit signed value and ignoring the sign so to speak.

results.title: Acceptance Criteria vs. Definition of Done: A Clear Distinction | by AydinSerbest | Medium
results.content:
Title: Acceptance Criteria vs. Definition of Done: A Clear Distinction | by AydinSerbest | Medium
In software development, both **Acceptance Criteria** and **Definition of Done (DoD)** are crucial, yet they are often confused due to their shared focus on **quality and completeness**. The modern software industry thrives on **“Release Early, Release Often.”** Agile methodologies, particularly Scrum, have made frequent releases the norm. The **iterative and incremental** Sprint-based model aligns with this, as highlighted in the **Scrum Guide (2020)**:. *“The entire Scrum Team is accountable for creating a valuable, useful Increment every Sprint.”*. The **Scrum Guide** defines DoD as:. *“A formal description of the state of the Increment when it meets the quality measures required for the product.”*. A Product Backlog Item (PBI) **cannot be released** or even presented in **Sprint Review** if it **does not meet** the DoD. *“Acceptance Criteria are the conditions that a product, user story, or increment of work must satisfy to be complete. In short, **Acceptance Criteria define the functional expectations** of a specific item. **Key Differences Between DoD and Acceptance Criteria**. **1️-DoD is part of Scrum; Acceptance Criteria is not mandatory**. * Acceptance Criteria is not a core Scrum practice but is widely adopted to ensure clarity. * DoD applies at a high level (macro), ensuring quality for all PBIs before they can be part of an Increment. * Acceptance Criteria is item-specific (micro), defining functional expectations unique to each PBI. * DoD ensures that an Increment is releasable and can include both functional and non-functional quality aspects (e.g., security, performance, documentation). * Acceptance Criteria define the expected functionality and user outcomes for a specific PBI. 👉 While DoD is universal, Acceptance Criteria vary for each PBI and are typically written within the “Definition” section of a Product Backlog Item. **Acceptance Criteria (Specific to this PBI)**. * ✅ All Acceptance Criteria are met. * ✅ Integration tests are completed with no failures. * ✅ **Manual testing** has been performed. * ✅ **Cross-browser testing** completed (Chrome, Firefox, Edge, Safari). * ✅ **Security tests** completed (OWASP Top 10 vulnerabilities scanned). * ✅ Product Owner has **approved** the feature for release. 🔹 **Acceptance Criteria help define the functional scope of each Product Backlog Item.**. 🔹 **Definition of Done ensures all Increments meet the required quality standards.**.

results.title: How to Handle Issues in Software Development Contracts: Clear ...
results.content: Published Time: 2025-04-29T05:04:42+00:00 How to Handle Issues in Software Development Contracts: Clear Communication - Attorney Aaron Hall How to Handle Issues in Software Development Contracts: Clear Communication Handling issues in software development contracts hinges on transparent communication. * Identifying Common Challenges in Software Development Contracts * Documenting Changes and Agreements Effectively * Utilizing Mediation and Conflict Resolution Techniques * Setting Realistic Expectations and Milestones * How Do Legal Jurisdictions Affect Software Development Contracts? Identifying Common Challenges in Software Development Contracts Although software development contracts aim to clearly define project scope and responsibilities, they frequently encounter challenges such as ambiguous requirements, scope creep, and unclear intellectual property rights. Clear definitions and measurable standards within contracts serve as critical tools to mitigate misunderstandings and ensure accountability throughout the development process. Clear definitions and measurable standards within software development contracts reduce misunderstandings but rely heavily on effective communication throughout the project lifecycle. Documenting Changes and Agreements Effectively Documenting changes and agreements promptly ensures alignment and prevents disputes in software development contracts. Utilizing Mediation and Conflict Resolution Techniques Employing mediation and conflict resolution techniques provides an effective pathway to address disputes in software development contracts without escalating to litigation. Implementing clear protocols for mediation early in the contract can prevent misunderstandings and promote timely resolution. Setting realistic expectations and milestones is crucial in software development contracts to prevent misunderstandings and delays. * Defining realistic timelines based on thorough project assessment * Breaking deliverables into manageable milestones with clear criteria * Regularly reviewing progress to implement milestone adjustments as needed * Documenting all changes transparently to maintain accountability ### How Do Legal Jurisdictions Affect Software Development Contracts? To mitigate risks, parties should clearly specify the governing jurisdiction and consider legal consultation to ensure the contract aligns with relevant jurisdictional requirements and interpretations. Key contract clauses to protect intellectual property in software development include clear definitions of ownership rights, specifying whether the client or developer retains ownership of code and deliverables. Additionally, clauses addressing the assignment of inventions and work-for-hire ensure that intellectual property created during the project belongs to the contracting party. Non-disclosure agreements (NDAs) in software development contracts safeguard confidential information by legally binding parties to maintain secrecy.
